name: Clobetasol skin lightening misuse

lead: Clobetasol propionate is a super-high-potency topical corticosteroid prescribed for conditions such as psoriasis, eczema and lichen sclerosus. In some markets it is also an ingredient in skin-lightening creams, where users apply it with the aim of a lighter, more even complexion.

The appearance goal is a paler skin tone or the fading of dark patches. Dermatology reviews describe the practice mainly in terms of its consequences: skin thinning, visible capillaries, acne, stretch marks and, with heavy use over large areas, effects on the body's own steroid production.

paras: Where it occurs, the steroid is typically one component of a commercially sold lightening cream applied daily to the face or body, sometimes mixed with other lightening agents such as hydroquinone or mercury compounds. Products sold illegally have been reported to contain higher concentrations than prescription formulations.

Reported effects include skin atrophy and bruising, telangiectasia, acne, permanent stretch marks, raised blood pressure and blood sugar, and suppression of the body's natural steroids. In the US clobetasol is prescription-only and has not been approved for skin whitening; the European Union does not allow corticosteroids in cosmetics.

angle.text: Users and sellers of lightening creams that contain clobetasol are aiming for a lighter, more even-looking skin tone. Medical sources describe the same ingredient mainly through the skin and systemic effects that follow regular use.

lead: Clobetasol skin lightening misuse refers to the use of clobetasol propionate, a prescription corticosteroid, as an active ingredient in creams marketed or used to lighten skin tone. Clobetasol belongs to the super-high-potency group of the US topical corticosteroid classification and is prescribed for inflammatory skin conditions including psoriasis, eczema, lichen sclerosus and alopecia areata.[1]

People who use such creams generally do so for the same reason as other skin-lightening products: to reach a lighter or more uniform complexion or to reduce the look of dark patches. Steroid-containing creams are one of several categories of lightening product that dermatology and public-health sources describe, alongside hydroquinone and mercury-containing creams.[2]

Published descriptions of the practice focus on its adverse effects, which include skin thinning, easy bruising, visible small blood vessels, acne, stretch marks and, with heavy long-term use over large areas, systemic steroid effects.[1][2] Regulators differ in how they treat these products: the US does not permit non-prescription sales, and the EU prohibits corticosteroids in cosmetics.[1][2]
infobox: Prescription-only; not FDA-approved for skin whitening[1]

paras: Clobetasol propionate is applied to the skin as a cream, ointment, gel, foam, solution or shampoo and is a first-line treatment for several inflammatory skin diseases.[1] In skin-lightening use, it is found as an undeclared or declared component of creams sold in beauty-supply shops and online.[1]

Corticosteroids are not lightening agents in the way hydroquinone is described. Reports on the practice describe steroid creams being included in products intended to improve complexion, and users in affected markets use them daily over the face or body.[1][2]

Survey figures cited for skin-lightening products overall are large: more than 25 percent of women in a number of African countries are reported to use them regularly, and about 40 percent of women in parts of Asia.[2] These figures cover all product types and are not specific to clobetasol.

In the US, clobetasol is prescription-only, the FDA has not approved it for skin whitening, and sales without a prescription are illegal, though creams containing it have been reported in New York City beauty-supply stores and online.[1] Some countries do not require a prescription for it.[1] The European Union does not allow corticosteroids in cosmetics because of their side-effect profile.[2]

Adverse effects described for clobetasol in general include skin irritation, dryness, redness, acne-like pimples and telangiectasia, while serious effects include allergic reactions, cellulitis, adrenal suppression and Cushing's syndrome.[1]

In the lightening context, sources list skin thinning and fragility, bruising, visible capillaries, acne, stretch marks that may be permanent, raised blood pressure and blood sugar, and suppression of natural steroid production, with higher absorption when used over large areas for long periods.[1][2] Reviews also note possible glaucoma, cataracts, edema, osteoporosis, menstrual irregularities and growth suppression in the most extensive use.[2]
No studies found of clobetasol as a skin-lightening treatment. Research on the practice consists of case reports and surveys of lightening-product use in general.
